name: The Endowment Effect
statement: We value a thing more once we own it.
meaning: People tend to value a good they own more highly than an identical good they do not own. In practice, the least someone will accept to give up an item exceeds the most they would pay to acquire the same item — a gap between willingness to accept and willingness to pay. Ownership itself inflates perceived value.
mechanism: The leading explanation is loss aversion applied to ownership, working through reference dependence: outcomes are judged as gains or losses relative to a reference point, here the state of owning the item. For an owner, parting with the good is coded as a loss, which looms large; for a buyer, acquiring it is coded as a gain, which weighs less. So the owner's valuation sits higher than the buyer's, even for the very same object. Competing accounts appeal to mere attachment or to expectation-based reference points.

examples.text: In the classic experiments, students randomly given a mug demanded about twice as much to sell it as other students, randomly assigned as buyers, would pay for it — random assignment ruling out that mugs went to those who valued them more.
People endowed with one good and offered an equal-value alternative trade far less often than standard theory predicts, as if giving up what they hold registers as a loss.
In field studies of collectors and traders, the effect shrank with market experience and was largely absent among seasoned dealers — a key challenge to its universality.

variants.name: The willingness-to-accept gap
variants.text: The operational signature of the effect — the systematic excess of the price owners demand to sell over the price buyers will pay for the identical good.

variants.name: Status quo bias
variants.text: The related preference for the current state of affairs, grouped with the endowment effect as reference-dependent anomalies of choice.

whyItMatters: It is a central finding of behavioural economics, challenging the standard assumption that a good's value is independent of who happens to own it. It bears on trade, markets, negotiation, and the design of default options and property rights — and it became a focal point in the debate over how robust behavioural anomalies really are.

working.text: anticipate that people will demand more to give up what they hold than others will pay for it, complicating trades and negotiations.
recognise that once something is possessed or set as the default, people cling to it, so defaults carry real weight.
remember the effect can shrink with market experience and can be affected by how a valuation is elicited, so it is not a fixed constant.

limits: The core phenomenon — a systematic gap between selling and buying prices in controlled experiments — is well replicated, but its cause and generality are genuinely contested. Market experience attenuates and can eliminate it, as List's field experiments with traders showed, suggesting part of it is novice inexperience. Plott and Zeiler argue the gap can be turned on and off by experimental procedure, implying it may partly reflect subjects' misconceptions about the elicitation rather than a true ownership effect. It is also weaker or absent for goods held for exchange. It should be presented as a real finding with a contested mechanism and contested robustness.
misreadings: It is not a universal, settled law of valuation — market experience and experimental design can shrink or remove it, and serious critics dispute how much is a genuine ownership effect. And it is distinct from the related IKEA effect, the extra value people place on things they built themselves.
origin: Named by Richard Thaler in 'Toward a Positive Theory of Consumer Choice' (1980); demonstrated in the coffee-mug experiments of Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch, and Richard Thaler, published in 1990.

sources.text: Endowment effect, Wikipedia. — the ownership-valuation statement, the mug experiments, and the List and Plott-Zeiler critiques.
Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler, "Experimental Tests of the Endowment Effect and the Coase Theorem," Journal of Political Economy 98(6):1325-1348 (1990).
